questions.q: In Qiskit's design, what IS a QuantumCircuit object, fundamentally?
options: A compiled, non-inspectable unit of computation, identical in nature to a Q# operation
A mutable, inspectable Python object -- data you build up, draw, transpile, or compose, with its existence as data being the core design point
A fixed hardware description that cannot be changed once created
A classical-only object with no connection to quantum gates
questions.explain: Qiskit's design makes the circuit itself a first-class, inspectable, mutable Python object -- you can draw it, count its depth, transpile it, or compose it with other circuits, all as operations on data.

questions.q: What does a Q# `operation` lack that a Qiskit `QuantumCircuit` has, according to the lesson?
options: The ability to apply any quantum gates at all
An intermediate, inspectable runtime object sitting between the written code and the actual computation -- there's no `.draw()` or `.depth()` equivalent on a compiled operation
Any way to allocate qubits
Any connection to the Azure Quantum resource estimator
questions.explain: A Q# operation is a compiled unit of computation, not a data object you inspect or transform at runtime the way a QuantumCircuit is -- that's the structural tradeoff the lesson draws out.

questions.q: What does Q#'s compiler-enforced model guarantee that Qiskit's `.inverse()`/`.control()` do not, per the lesson?
options: Nothing -- the two approaches provide identical guarantees

That an operation declared is Adj + Ctl is checked and correctly derived by the compiler itself, whereas Qiskit's .inverse()/.control() are library implementations with no type-system guarantee that a custom gate behaves correctly under them
That Qiskit circuits can never contain bugs
That Q# programs run faster than Qiskit programs
questions.explain: The lesson is specific: Q#'s functors are compiler-checked and compiler-derived from the operation's own structure, while Qiskit's equivalents are library-level conveniences with no type-system guarantee for custom gates.

questions.q: What does Qiskit's circuit-as-data model make naturally easy that Q#'s model does not, according to the lesson?
options: Compiler-enforced separation between classical and quantum code
Circuit introspection and transformation -- transpilation, drawing, programmatically composing circuits as literal data operations at runtime
Automatically deriving an operation's inverse without writing any code
Preventing measurement from being called inside a pure function
questions.explain: Because the circuit is just inspectable Python data, operations like transpilation, visualization, and runtime composition fall out naturally -- a genuine strength of Qiskit's model that Q#'s compiled operations don't provide in the same way.

questions.q: According to the lesson, is one of the two language models more 'capable' in terms of which algorithms it can express?
options: Yes, Q# can express strictly more algorithms than Qiskit
Yes, Qiskit can express strictly more algorithms than Q#

No -- both can express the same algorithms (as demonstrated across this course); the real difference is what the language does for you by construction (compiler guarantees vs. dynamic object manipulation), not raw expressive capability
Neither language can express Grover's algorithm or teleportation
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that the same algorithms were implemented in both tools across this learning path -- the difference is the programming model's tradeoffs, not which algorithms are expressible at all.
